extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in an introductory proof-writing / discrete mathematics course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing clear, rigorous undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (direct proofs, combinatorial proofs, pigeonhole arguments, case analysis) and for using/being precise with definitions and accepted facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must be understandable and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a theorem is a written verification that shows that the theorem is definitely and unequivocally true. A proof should be understandable and convincing to anyone who has the requisite background and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the intended reader has the background to follow definitions, notation, and logical steps. Use clear logical progression and state assumptions. The proof should leave no ambiguity about why the conclusion follows from the premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguity; agree on exact meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial that both the writer of the proof and the readers of the proof agree on the exact meanings of all the words, for otherwise there is an intolerable level of ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State or reference precise definitions for any mathematical terms used. If a term is used without definition, ensure it is standard and understood by the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions concretely in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is an exact, unambiguous explanation of the meaning of a mathematical word or phrase. It is common to express definitions as conditional statements even though the biconditional would more appropriately convey the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a hypothesis invokes a definition (e.g., 'x is odd'), rewrite it in the concrete form given by the definition (e.g., x = 2a + 1) and use that algebraically. Be aware that definitions are intended biconditionally even if written as 'If...then...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for direct proof (assume P, prove Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional 'If P, then Q', begin by assuming P and show this forces Q to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with 'Suppose P.' and end with 'Therefore Q.' Fill the intervening steps using logic, definitions and accepted facts. This is the standard template for direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write first and last lines first, then fill the middle
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s generally a good idea to write the first and last line of your proof first, and then fill in the gap, sometimes jumping alternately between top and bottom until you meet in the middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical method helps focus the proof: sketch 'Suppose P' and 'Therefore Q' then derive intermediate equations/implications. Use scratch work as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid variable name conflicts; rename parameters when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying definitions that introduce new parameters, avoid reusing letters already in use in different roles; use new letters to prevent confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a|b gives b = a d and 'c' is already used, pick d or e instead. Explicitly state the new variable's domain (e.g., d ∈ ℤ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard algebraic/manipulative facts without reproving
rubrics_metrics.description: We accept and use such things as the distributive and commutative properties of addition and multiplication, as well as other standard properties of arithmetic and algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference these standard properties as needed rather than re-proving them; rely on them to transform expressions (e.g., expand (2a+1)^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept certain foundational facts as given
rubrics_metrics.description: Some standard results (e.g., Division Algorithm, unique prime factorization) are accepted without proof (at least initially) and may be used in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using such facts, either cite them by name or ensure the audience expects them as background. Be prepared to revisit or justify them later if required by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof: show two expressions count the same set
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial proof is a method of proving two different expressions are equal by showing that they are both answers to the same counting question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a combinatorial set S and show each expression counts some natural partitioning or pairing of S. Examples: proving Pascal's identity by partitioning k-subsets by whether they contain 0; proving sum of squares of binomial coefficients equals central binomial coefficient by counting n-element subsets of a 2n set partitioned into A and B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use partitioning and pairing in combinatorial arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When counting, partition sets by a distinguishing property (e.g., contains 0 or not), or pair objects via a bijection (e.g., complement mapping X ↔ S − X) to derive identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition arguments often yield sums of binomial coefficients; pairing arguments can show symmetry such as C(n,k) = C(n,n−k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the multiplication principle for composite choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When selections are made in independent stages (e.g., choose k from A and n−k from B), use the multiplication principle to multiply counts of each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to derive product terms in combinatorial sums; justify independence of stages before applying multiplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (division principle) — set up boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide items into boxes; if there are more items than boxes, some box contains more than one item. Use ceiling/floor reasoning to quantify guaranteed counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe the boxes (e.g., months, colors, subtriangles). Use ceiling(n/boxes) to guarantee at least that many in some box. Examples: 13 people into 12 months ⇒ two share a month; 49 gumballs among 4 colors ⇒ ceiling(49/4)=13 of same color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averaging viewpoint for pigeonhole results
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of explicitly using boxes, one can use averages: the average count per category is n/boxes; if the average exceeds k, some category has at least k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an equivalent, often more compact, presentation of the division principle; show small examples to illustrate (e.g., gumballs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis when a property behaves differently across possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement's truth depends on properties like parity or sign, split the proof into exhaustive cases (e.g., n even or odd) and prove the claim in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly label cases, handle each thoroughly, and ensure the cases cover all possibilities. Combine results to conclude the universal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat very similar cases together to avoid redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more cases lead to identical or nearly identical reasoning, combine them or handle them uniformly to streamline the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group similar parity/sign cases or use a unified argument that covers multiple cases when appropriate (section 'Treating Similar Cases').

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove equality of two quantities, show both inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can prove m ≤ n and n ≤ m separately, then it follows that m = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate arguments for each direction; the techniques for each inequality can differ. Example: showing lcm(ca,cb) = c·lcm(a,b) by proving ≤ and ≥.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure legality of operations that might change inequality direction
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating inequalities (e.g., taking square roots), verify the preconditions (non-negativity) so the operation doesn't reverse or invalidate the inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If taking square roots, ensure both sides are non-negative (or cite a prior proposition that justifies taking square roots without reversing ≤). Example: from 4xy ≤ (x+y)^2 deduce 2√(xy) ≤ x+y because both sides are non-negative for positive x,y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide witnesses in existence proofs (constructive by cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving existence (e.g., 'there is n such that ...'), explicitly produce a value (witness) often selected by cases (zero, positive, negative) and verify it works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the explicit formula or construction for n in each case and check the equality/condition. Example: showing every multiple of 4 equals 1+(−1)^n(2n−1) by choosing n based on sign of a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write final proofs in paragraph form and use standard markers
rubrics_metrics.description: While line-by-line steps are useful in scratch work, final proofs are typically written cleanly in paragraph form, beginning with 'Proof.' and ending with a box or symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite staged proofs into coherent paragraphs once the logical flow is clear; keep clarity and explicit references to definitions/facts used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear set and combinatorial notation and explain counting viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing combinatorial proofs, clearly identify the set being counted and the combinatorial interpretation of each algebraic term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, describe S, A, B and how (n choose k) counts k-subsets; explain partitions or selection strategies that correspond to terms in an identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to test sharpness of bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bound is claimed to be minimal or tight, provide or consider explicit examples showing that smaller values fail (e.g., picking 5 numbers might avoid a sum of 9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these examples to justify minimality or necessity of hypotheses (e.g., n=48 gumballs can fail because 12 of each color is possible).
